name: Southeast Ridge

rappel_detail.notes: The one rappel of the descent; it can also be downclimbed on belay. A 40 m rope is ideal and a 30 m reaches. Below it, descend the long gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: webbing/sling anchor just above the chockstone (heavily used; back it up)
hazards: The rope can catch on the chockstone on the pull, and you can pendulum if you rappel off to one side.
rappel_detail.station: The short, blocky cleft capped by a chockstone near the top of the South Gully, about 50 ft high.

rappels: One rappel of about 50 ft at the chockstone cleft near the top of the South Gully (or downclimb it on belay), then descend the gully on foot
descent_text: From the true summit, scramble back east along the summit ridge to the top of the South Gully. Its one technical step is a short, blocky rock cleft capped by a chockstone, with a fixed sling above it: rappel it or downclimb it on belay. Below that, descend the long gully and the brushy, forested slope beneath it toward Ingalls Creek, return to camp, and reverse the approach over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. The descent is long, so leave the summit with a comfortable margin of daylight.
approach: Start at the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (roughly 3,650 ft). At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike/Beverly Creek Trail) — do not miss this junction, as a wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek Trail is a commonly reported mistake. Continue to roughly 3.1 miles and turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail), climbing to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles (roughly 5,900-6,000 ft), which opens up the first real views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. From the pass, descend the well-maintained trail on the far side to the south shore of Ingalls Creek at about 6 miles (roughly 4,200-4,250 ft); ford the creek (wading or a footlog depending on the season/year) to reach flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence. From camp, leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb generally north into the gentle, heather-and-slab Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side, working up open basin terrain beside the southeast ridge, the crest that rises from this side to the southeast spire. The roped climbing follows that crest, about eight pitches to the southeast spire. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford can be a real obstacle in early season or after rain; the basin approach involves loose talus and, in shoulder season, hard snow that may warrant an axe and crampons; this is a long, remote approach (partial day just to reach the base) so plan for a car-camp or bivy.
overview: The Southeast Ridge of Argonaut gives a longer and slightly more technical line to the summit than the northeast ridge, climbing the rocky crest over a series of steps and towers on excellent Stuart Range granite. With sustained moderate climbing, real exposure, and a remote setting, it rewards parties willing to make the long approach into this quieter corner of the range. Route-finding among the towers is part of the challenge and the fun.
beta: Climbs the southeast ridge in about eight pitches up to 5.6 to the southeast spire, a false summit and the lowest of Argonaut's three summits, then carries on to the true summit on the west spire. The lower pitches are blocky and awkward, carry a lot of lichen and are somewhat hard to protect. The line includes two single-rope rappels, or one double-rope rappel, into the notch. The main summit needs a short, non-exposed Class 4 move to its highest block after Class 3 ridge traversing. The Colchuck Col side is the better way to the base; the Ingalls Creek side means a long, strenuous bushwhack.
